articles.title: These Google Pixel Phones No Longer Receive Software Support
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Marinel Sigue)
articles.content:
These Google Pixel Phones No Longer Receive Software Support
There are usually two major problems with old Google Pixel phones: degraded battery and discontinued software support. The battery issue can be resolved by getting a battery replacement for around $119 at a Google Store. But for the software support, phones are considered end-of-life once official updates stop. That's now the case for some Pixel phones. Every Google Pixel model from the Pixel 1 through the Pixel 5 series no longer gets official updates, meaning no more new features or security patches.
At this point, you have three options. You're free to still use the device as is, but without security updates, you'll soon find yourself in a vulnerable spot. Your device becomes more prone to malware, viruses, and hackers, and apps might stop working too. If you're comfortable tinkering with your phone's software, you can go with the custom OS route instead. This known loophole to unlock new updates for old Android phones essentially involves installing a completely new operating system on your device. It's a straightforward process, but can get quite technical. If you prefer to skip all that hassle, you can always upgrade to the newer Google Pixel phones that are still officially supported.
Which Google Pixel phones still get updates?
In terms of software support, recently released Google Pixel phones can last seven years. So if you have a Pixel 8 and newer, you won't have to worry about missing out on any future Android updates. Google guarantees both OS and security updates for these devices for seven years from the date of their U.S. release. To be more specific, here's the end-of-life date for your Android phone, based on the model:
- Pixel 10a: March 2033
- Pixel 10 Pro Fold: October 2032
- Pixel 10, 10 Pro, and 10 Pro XL: August 2032
- Pixel 9a: April 2032
- Pixel 9 Pro and 9 Pro Fold: September 2031
- Pixel 9 and 9 Pro XL: August 2031
- Pixel 8a: May 2031
- Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro: October 2030
Models newer than the Pixel 5 but older than the Pixel 8 still get updates today as well. But instead of seven years, they only receive five years of software support. Here's when these models will stop receiving updates:
- Pixel Fold: June 2028
- Pixel 7a: May 2028
- Pixel 7 and 7 Pro: October 2027
- Pixel 6a: July 2027
- Pixel 6 and 6 Pro: October 2026
That said, even though software support for these Google Pixel models is said to last five or seven years, don't expect to automatically get every single feature in the Pixel Drops. Some of them are hardware-specific and might not be compatible with every model.
articles.summary:
Google has officially ended software and security update support for all Pixel smartphone models ranging from the original Pixel through the Pixel 5 series.

### Key Points
- Google Pixel 1 through Pixel 5 devices no longer receive official Android OS updates or critical security patches.
- Users of unsupported devices face increased risks from malware and potential incompatibility with modern mobile applications.
- Owners can continue using older devices, install custom operating systems, or upgrade to newer models to maintain security.
- Google now guarantees seven years of software support for the Pixel 8 series and newer devices released in the United States.
- Models released between the Pixel 6 and Pixel 7 series receive five years of support, with expiration dates ranging from 2026 to 2028.

### Why it Matters
The discontinuation of support for older hardware highlights the growing importance of long-term software commitments in the smartphone industry. Consumers must now weigh the longevity of update cycles when purchasing devices to avoid security vulnerabilities and premature hardware obsolescence.

articles.title: Trump’s media company reports $238m loss
articles.author: Erin Hale
articles.content:
US President Donald Trump’s media conglomerate has reported a net loss of $238m in the second quarter of 2026, against revenue of $1.7m.
In its latest filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Monday, Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) attributed most of the shortfall to $190.4m in unrealised losses on digital assets, digital assets pledged and equity securities.

Other losses included $11.7m in “accreted interest” – unpaid interest on a loan that is added to the principal – and $8.1m in “stock-based compensation”.
TMTG said revenue for the April-June quarter rose 89 percent compared with the same period last year, though losses continued to outpace earnings.
Almost all of TMTG’s revenue came from “media segments”, including $1.43m from advertising and $179,500 from subscriptions, according to the SEC filings.
The financial results bring TMTG’s net losses for the first half of 2026 to $644m, against revenue of $2.5m.
Shares of TMTG, which trades under the NASDAQ symbol “DJT”, were down 8 percent at market closing on Monday.
TMTG’s portfolio includes the social media platform Truth Social, the video streaming service Truth+ and the fintech brand Truth.Fi.
Over the past year, the company has also branched into other areas, including cryptocurrency and, as of August 1, market intelligence through the controversial subscription service Truth API.
Truth API provides investors faster access to posts on Truth Social, where Trump regularly makes market-moving announcements on policy issues such as tariffs and the US-Israel war on Iran.
TMTG interim CEO Kevin McGurn said during an earnings call on Monday that 10 companies had already signed up for the service, which has raised conflict of interest concerns, paying $60,000 to $100,000 per month in fees.
Despite the influence of Trump’s posts, Truth Social has lagged behind rival platforms such as X and Facebook in terms of users since its launch in 2022.
The New York Times reported on Monday that visitors to Truth Social in July were down by more than a third compared with the same period last year, citing data from the online tracking firm Similarweb.
articles.summary:
Trump Media & Technology Group reported a $238 million net loss for the second quarter of 2026, driven largely by unrealized losses on digital assets and equity securities.

### Key Points
- TMTG recorded $1.7 million in revenue for the quarter, an 89 percent increase compared to the same period in 2025.
- The company’s total net losses for the first half of 2026 reached $644 million against $2.5 million in total revenue.
- Unrealized losses on digital assets and equity securities accounted for $190.4 million of the quarterly shortfall.
- Shares of the company, trading under the ticker "DJT," fell 8 percent following the Monday filing with the SEC.
- The firm’s new Truth API service, which provides early access to market-moving posts, has secured 10 corporate clients paying monthly fees up to $100,000.
- Similarweb data indicates that visitor traffic to the Truth Social platform declined by more than one-third in July compared to the previous year.

### Why it Matters
The widening gap between TMTG’s operational costs and revenue highlights the financial volatility inherent in the company's business model. Investors remain focused on whether the firm can successfully monetize its influence through new ventures like Truth API while navigating declining user engagement on its core social platform.

articles.title: GoPro Searches for a Lifeline as It Lost $51 Million Last Quarter
articles.author: Jeremy Gray
articles.content:
GoPro has announced its second-quarter financial results and some of the core numbers are dire.
Despite launching the all-new Mission 1 Series cameras earlier this year, decidedly good cameras no less, it has been a tough 2026 for GoPro, following years of difficulties dealing with growing Chinese competitors.
GoPro said in April that it would lay off about 23 percent of its workforce this year amid excess costs. The company disclosed the following month that it was evaluating its options, including contemplating a potential sale.
Last month, GoPro’s founder and CEO, Nicholas Woodman, effectively lent the company $20 million. Just a couple of weeks later, NASDAQ warned the company that it was no longer compliant with listing requirements. As of writing, GoPro’s stock is trading at just 70 cents a share, a far cry from its peak share price of $94 in October 2014.
Today’s financial results paint a dismal picture for the American camera company that was once at the top of the action camera industry. Hardware revenue is down 39.9 percent year-over-year while subscription and services revenue is up 10.6 percent. Overall revenue is down 31.3 percent.
GoPro says it sold approximately 291,000 camera units last quarter, which is down 38 percent year-over-year. While the GoPro Mission 1 and Mission 1 Pro launched at the end of May, just a month before the second quarter ended, it’s very bad news that the exciting launch didn’t offer more relief for GoPro.
With GAAP accounting, GoPro lost $51 million, or 30 cents per share, in the second quarter. In the same period last year, GoPro lost $16 million. The company’s non-GAAP net loss was $36 million, compared to $12 million in Q2 last year. With either accounting method, the loss is dramatic.
As GoPro reiterated today, the company’s Board of Directors authorized a process to evaluate a potential sale of GoPro and other strategic options, all to maximize shareholder value.
“The inquiries we have received span the defense, consumer and financial sectors, and we are in the later stages of the process. As I’ve shared, this process has my full support,” says Nicholas Woodman.
“To close, looking back at Q2, we expanded the performance and creative potential of our camera lineup with the launch of the Mission 1 Series of cameras and continued to make progress with our strategic review process that aims to maximize shareholder value,” Woodman concluded.
“I’m very proud of our team’s execution and I’m excited about our new and upcoming products as they further establish GoPro as one of the world’s most exciting digital imaging companies and brands.”

articles.summary:
GoPro reported a 31.3 percent decline in overall revenue for the second quarter of 2026 as the company faces mounting financial losses and explores a potential corporate sale.

### Key Points
- GoPro reported a $51 million GAAP net loss for the second quarter, significantly higher than the $16 million loss recorded during the same period last year.
- Total hardware revenue dropped 39.9 percent year-over-year, with camera unit sales falling 38 percent to approximately 291,000 units.
- CEO Nicholas Woodman provided a $20 million loan to the company, which is currently facing non-compliance warnings from NASDAQ.
- The company previously announced a 23 percent workforce reduction earlier this year to address rising operational costs.
- GoPro’s Board of Directors is currently evaluating strategic options, including a potential sale, with inquiries received from the defense, consumer, and financial sectors.

### Why it Matters
GoPro’s struggle to maintain market share against low-cost Chinese competitors highlights the volatility of the action camera industry. The company's ongoing strategic review and potential sale signal a critical turning point for a brand that once dominated the digital imaging market.

articles.title: Anker’s travel charger works in almost any country and is down to $20
articles.author: Sheena Vasani
articles.content:
If you’ve got international travel coming up, an adapter is essential for keeping your phone, earbuds, power banks, and other gadgets charged. Anker’s Nano Travel Adapter is one of our picks from our guide to the best gadgets for summer travel because it can charge up to five devices at once, yet it’s small enough to fit in the palm of your hand. It’s also available in black for just $19.99 ($6 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Anker (with code WS7DV2BNB82J) matching its best price to date.
Anker’s travel charger works in almost any country and is down to $20
The adapter can power up to five devices at once and is at its best price to date.
The Nano’s four built-in sets of prongs should keep you covered in “over 200 countries and regions,” according to Anker. It also features two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports, along with an AC outlet for plugging in a standard wall charger. A single USB-C port delivers up to 20W, which should be enough to get an iPhone 17 to 50 percent in less than 30 minutes. That’s not enough power to charge most laptops, making the USB ports better suited for smaller gadgets like phones, tablets, earbuds, and power banks. You can still charge your laptop, however, by plugging its wall charger into the AC outlet.
What’s more, it’s designed to take up as little space as possible. The adapter’s only an inch thick with its prongs folded in and, at 3.8 ounces, weighs less than a smartphone. Just keep in mind that the Nano doesn’t convert voltage, so you’ll want to make sure gadgets like hair dryers and electric razors support the voltage at your destination before plugging them in.

articles.title: No evidence of data breach after Chinese-made component found in Navy drones, MoD says
articles.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
articles.content:
- Published
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said there is no evidence to suggest a systems or data breach after the Royal Navy's new sea drones were found to include a Chinese-made component.
During what the MoD called a "routine cyber vulnerability assessment" of the drones, the cameras were found to have sent a squark – also known as a heartbeat communication – to a Chinese IP address.
A squark can signal when the system is switched on, is functioning properly, but it can also carry location information.
"A thorough investigation found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally," an MoD spokesperson said.
"Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment," the MoD added.
This is embarrassing for the MoD which, like most Nato countries, has banned Chinese components from military equipment - not least over fears of spying.
The K3 Scout sea drones can remotely carry out surveillance, and according to their supplier, "support a wide range of mission profiles including maritime awareness, force protection, logistics and precision strike".
The supplier of the Royal Navy's 20 new K3 sea drones, Kraken, said it was given assurances about security. But a third party supplier of the drone camera still had Chinese-made components.
Kraken has said it is confident no sensitive information has been shared.
The story was first reported by The Telegraph., external
The security lapse has been addressed, but it is a reminder of the heavy dominance on Chinese supply chains.
Even the defence sector – which has taken measures to prevent espionage – still struggles to source materials, and technologies that are China free, or as cheap.
articles.summary:
The UK Ministry of Defence confirmed that Chinese-made components found in new Royal Navy K3 Scout sea drones did not result in any data breaches or security compromises.

### Key Points
- Routine vulnerability assessments revealed that drone cameras were transmitting heartbeat signals to a Chinese IP address.
- The Ministry of Defence stated that no sensitive military data or systems were accessed or transmitted during the incident.
- Kraken, the supplier of the 20 K3 Scout drones, confirmed the Chinese components originated from a third-party camera manufacturer.
- NATO nations maintain strict policies banning Chinese-made components in military equipment due to ongoing espionage and national security concerns.
- The security lapse has been addressed, though the incident highlights the difficulty of removing Chinese technology from global defense supply chains.

### Why it Matters
This incident underscores the significant challenges defense agencies face in auditing complex global supply chains for hidden foreign components. It highlights the persistent tension between sourcing cost-effective technology and maintaining the rigorous security standards required for sensitive military equipment.

articles.title: Cybersecurity stocks hit record highs, and one analyst target lasted a morning
articles.author: Cristian Dina
articles.content:
CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks hit record highs on Monday. Each rose more than 5%, after a week in which the Black Hat conference in Las Vegas turned into an argument about AI agents.
CNBC’s Samantha Subin reported the move. CrowdStrike gained 11.32 points, or 5.28%. Palo Alto added 17.84 points, or 4.90%, and traded at $381.70 in the afternoon.
The rest of the sector followed. Tenable and Rubrik rose more than 7%. Netskope and Zscaler each gained about 5%.
A price target overtaken the same day
BTIG lifted its price target on Palo Alto to $380 on Monday. The firm called that about 4% upside from Friday’s close.
The stock passed it within hours. Palo Alto changed hands at $381.70 that afternoon, above a target raised the same morning. Buyers are repricing this sector faster than the analysts who cover it.
CrowdStrike’s target went to $237, which BTIG put at 11% upside from Friday. Rubrik went to $109. None of the three revisions followed an earnings release.
What changed at Black Hat
BTIG’s analysts spent the conference talking to partners, vendors and customers. The consistent theme, they wrote, was that AI agents “have fundamentally changed the threat landscape.”
They called the environment meaningfully worse than before. They also said the deployment of AI security tools sits “only in the early innings”.
Cantor’s analysts reached a similar view. AI has moved “from being a cybersecurity feature to a key pillar” of both the attack surface and the infrastructure on either side of it, they wrote.
The trade has a name on television too. Jefferies analyst Joseph Gallo argued last week that cyber spending will benefit from AI anxiety over the next couple of quarters.
The week supplied its own evidence
Black Hat did not lack for demonstrations. Researchers used the conference to pick apart a Hugging Face breach carried out by an AI agent rather than a person.
The pattern is no longer theoretical. Security firms have already documented an end-to-end ransomware attack run by an agent from reconnaissance through to extortion.
Private money is moving on the same thesis. Mate Security raised $50m for AI-driven security operations during the same conference week.
What Monday does not prove
This was one trading session on sell-side commentary. Neither company reported results, and no customer contract was announced. Analyst notes move stocks, but they are not revenue.
There is a circularity worth naming. The companies whose shares rose are the ones selling the fix for the threat their own conference describes, and BTIG says that build-out has barely started.
Spending is also not the same as safety. Buying more tools has never closed the remediation gap between finding a problem and fixing it.
Palo Alto has its own unfinished argument here. Its chief executive Nikesh Arora has said AI token pricing must fall before the economics of agentic security work at scale.
The test arrives with results. Targets can be raised again, and often are, but the claim that AI has changed the threat landscape only pays off if customers spend against it. Until then, Monday’s records rest on a week of conversations in Las Vegas.

articles.summary:
Cybersecurity stocks including CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks reached record highs on Monday following industry discussions at the Black Hat conference regarding the evolving threat of AI agents.

### Key Points
- CrowdStrike shares rose 5.28% while Palo Alto Networks gained 4.90%, reaching a trading price of $381.70.
- BTIG analysts raised price targets for Palo Alto, CrowdStrike, and Rubrik, citing the fundamental shift in the threat landscape caused by AI.
- Security firms have documented real-world ransomware attacks executed by AI agents, moving the technology from theoretical to practical application.
- Other sector players including Tenable, Rubrik, Netskope, and Zscaler saw gains of approximately 5% to 7% during the trading session.
- Private security firm Mate Security secured $50 million in funding during the same week, highlighting increased investor interest in AI-driven defense tools.

### Why it Matters
The surge reflects growing market confidence that AI-driven security threats will force enterprises to increase their cybersecurity spending significantly. While these gains are currently driven by analyst sentiment rather than earnings, they underscore a broader industry transition toward AI as a central pillar of both digital infrastructure and defense.

articles.title: This New Open-Weight AI Model Is Built for Video and Robots
articles.author: Katelyn Chedraoui
articles.content:
While tech leaders continue to debate the merits and pitfalls of open-weight AI models, developers aren’t slowing down. LTX on Tuesday released the newest version of its open world model, called LTX-2.5.
LTX-2.5 is an open world model, which is different from most AIs you probably know. While LLMs are good at generating text, world models are complex webs that translate the physical world into a language that generative AI can understand. The idea is that the model has a grounded understanding of our world, so it hallucinates less. Think about robots that can navigate a room without bumping into anything, or AI video clips that know to have people walk around objects rather than fade through them like a poltergeist. You can use world models to simulate digital environments, generate content and help program robots.
The new model has improvements to reduce the number of visual artifacts (or errors) the AI makes, better consistency across generations thanks to a new pixel diffusion process. Because it’s an open model, companies can download and customize the model for their own needs; that helps keep their intellectual property safe. So a movie studio could use LTX-2.5 to create and edit video clips featuring their characters. LTX-2.5 is optimized for local inference on Nvidia’s RTX GPU, which means developers can run it on their own hardware and keep their work away from cloud-based AI services.
LTX-2.5 is available to download and use now on sites like HuggingFace and ComfyUI.
LTX is one of the most popular developers of open-weight AI models. LTX’s models have been downloaded more than 33 million times by HuggingFace users, including those who made their own versions based on LTX’s blueprints. OpenAI and Google each have a family of open-weight models, GPT-OSS and Gemma 4, respectively, though the companies’ number of closed models far outnumbers their open-weights ones. Anthropic has no open Claude models.
Open-source advocates have long argued that the best way forward is for tech companies to make public disclosures about how their tools work. That debate has only intensified in the AI era. Popular Chinese models are being released in open formats, like the new Kimi 3 from Moonshot, which gives developers, researchers and cybersecurity experts insights into how it works. When the Trump administration was reportedly considering banning Chinese and other foreign AI models in July because it was worried about cybersecurity threats, many industry leaders spoke up, saying such a move could actually threaten cybersecurity.
While most AI leaders say open-weights models shouldn’t be banned, the big players aren’t rushing to release many of these kinds of models. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is encouraging more open AI. He published a lengthy essay on Monday outlining his position that open-weight models will bring the “benefits of AI” to more people. Meta also released a new open-weights model called Muse Glimmer and promised to release the weights of another recent model, called Spark 1.2.
LTX has a similar philosophy. Neither government nor private companies would be good stewards of private AI models, CEO and co-founder Zeev Farbman wrote in a recent post. One is primarily motivated by ever-shifting political goals and the other by pure profit.
“It shouldn’t sit with a small number of decision makers, regardless of whether they’re in government or a limited number of powerful companies,” Farbman writes. “Decisions belong with the end users, through models they can control and inspect for themselves.”
articles.summary:
LTX has released LTX-2.5, an updated open-weight world model designed to improve visual consistency and reduce artifacts for developers building simulations, robotics, and generative video applications.

### Key Points
- LTX-2.5 utilizes a new pixel diffusion process to enhance visual accuracy and reduce errors in generated content.
- The model is optimized for local inference on Nvidia RTX GPUs, allowing developers to maintain data privacy without relying on cloud services.
- Users can download and customize the model via platforms including HuggingFace and ComfyUI.
- LTX models have surpassed 33 million downloads, positioning the company as a significant contributor to the open-weight AI ecosystem.
- The release aligns with a broader industry debate regarding the accessibility of AI technology versus the control maintained by major tech corporations.

### Why it Matters
This release provides developers with greater control over AI infrastructure by enabling local deployment and customization of complex world models. By bypassing cloud-based services, companies can protect their intellectual property while utilizing advanced tools for robotics and digital simulation.

articles.title: Legislation To Slow The Pace Of Frontier AI Could Spur A Highly Dangerous Preemptive Acceleration
articles.author:
Lance Eliot, Contributor, 
 Lance Eliot, Contributor
 https://www.forbes.com/sites/lanceeliot/
articles.content:
In today’s column, I examine the recent calls for using AI governance and new laws about AI to slow the pace of AI development. On the one hand, the rationale is that we ought to nail down AI safety before we allow AI to advance beyond our means of control. That certainly makes sense. But one tremendous downside is the likely “unanticipated adverse consequences” of seeking an across-the-board slowdown (it is not truly unanticipated since right here I share with you the expected consequences).
The gist is this. If things start to look like an actual slowdown of AI is going to be imposed, there will be a heightened frenzy to beat the deadline and proceed with tremendous haste. A sudden and wild rush will occur. I refer to this as a preemptive acceleration effect. We’ve seen this happen in other areas of impending regulation. Often, there is a pell-mell brawl before a new regulation takes effect. The question is whether the turmoil of preemptive acceleration might be so over-the-top that AI goes utterly awry and we suffer exceedingly more severe consequences than if we had left things alone. The said-to-be cure inadvertently causes immense calamity. It’s a real possibility and a real concern.
Let’s talk about it. This analysis of AI breakthroughs is part of my ongoing Forbes column coverage on the latest in AI, including identifying and explaining various impactful AI complexities (see the link here).
The Pace Of AI Advances
I’m sure that you gamely know that the pace of AI advancements is frenetic. Almost every day there is a new announcement about some resoundingly breathtaking AI innovation. Whereas this used to be a once-a-year kind of pronouncement, we have shifted to daily occurrences. Anyone who does doomscrolling on their smartphone can observe AI breakthrough announcements that arrive on nearly an hourly or minute-by-minute basis.
The ordinary reaction would be that this is an exciting time to be alive. We are all in the front row when it comes to AI advancing and changing our lives. Imagine that fifty years ago the world at large could only dream of such an amazing pace. And, perhaps fifty years from now, in the future, the whole kit-and-caboodle will have slowed down after we’ve already exhausted all feasible AI innovations (well, some believe there will be even more, due to AI generating discoveries on behalf of humans).
Here’s the problem at hand. The pace of technological advancement is outdoing the pace of figuring out how to handle the ramifications of this newest AI. Policies about guiding AI development and controlling its downsides are slowly being churned out. Laws that protect the public from runaway AI are only now being crafted and potentially put in place. The issue is that the AI tech advances are happening at lightning speeds and we are collectively far beyond the end of our skis. For my detailed coverage of this head-scratching conundrum, see the link here.
What To Do About The Pace
There is a tremendous amount of handwringing going on about the feverish pace of AI. A recent online letter signed by over a thousand AI frontier employees has sought to bring this matter to the attention of the public and policymakers; see my analysis of the situation at the link here. One perspective is that it is impossible to hold back progress. No matter what roadblocks or guideposts are erected, AI is going to be advanced. If one country decides to go slower, all that this will do is put themselves behind the times. They are going to be left in the dust.
An associated argument is made that if there is to be a slowing of the pace, this must be done universally. Everyone must agree with it. In that case, no country will get ahead of anyone else. No country will fall behind anyone else. The world will be at the same juncture when it comes to advancing AI. This is the proverbial kumbaya version of AI pacing.
A big question arises that makes the pacing consideration somewhat muddled. How can we know what the pace of AI is? In other words, suppose that all the countries of the globe agreed to slow down the pace of AI advancements. You cannot just naively assume that this will actually occur. It would require a practical means of detecting AI advancements, along with gauging the pace at which they are proceeding. I suppose you could liken this to nuclear missile agreements, namely that without a means of monitoring and measuring, any agreement limiting their proliferation is a mere paper-based “feel good” exercise.
Trying To Beat The Starting Gun
One phenomenon that rarely comes up when considering instituting a law that imposes a regulatory deadline or legal imposition is that there can be a huge preemptive effort to get something done under the wire. In the case of AI, it seems readily sensible that AI makers would opt to move heaven and earth to try and advance their AI prior to a legally required slowdown. This is human nature in action.
Ponder this. If you knew that everyone was going to be forced to reduce the pace of their AI development, wouldn’t you want to make sure that your AI is as advanced as humanly possible? Of course you would. Your desire would be to get the starting gate with the most advanced AI at that point in time. The slowdown then would only impact your AI from that already advanced level.
Think of the advantages. Your competition is going to be possibly behind your level of AI. They cannot try to speed things up once the slowdown is underway. They will likely be stuck perennially behind the advances of your AI. Nice. Shame on them for not having had the foresight to pick up the pace prior to the deadline. They weren’t paying attention. Too bad for them.
The Marketplace Rewards This Behavior
You can place a nearly sure bet that the marketplace would reward this type of behavior. Imagine that an AI maker has opted to speed up their advances and manages to do a bang-up job of doing so. They are doing this in anticipation of a proposed law that is nearing its final stages. The law isn’t yet in place. There is legal room to maneuver.
Bam, the new law passes, and the law stipulates that all AI advances must be undertaken at a measured pace. Great, we all feel safer. Meanwhile, the AI maker that pulled out all the stops has the best AI around. Nobody has AI as advanced as they do.
What would happen?
The marketplace would astutely gravitate to that AI. Might as well be at the top rung of AI. From then on, it’s a slugfest of making new advances that do not exceed the legally mandated pace. The AI maker has wisely guaranteed themselves excess market share and can even charge a premium for having astutely beaten the clock. To the victor go the spoils.
Rewind The Clock
It doesn’t seem likely that only one AI maker would anticipate the preemptive move. Other AI makers would almost certainly do the same. They want to become the chosen one. Therefore, we will have a widespread wild race of AI makers attempting to beat the clock.
You might be tempted to say that’s fine. It would be handy that they all try to make as many advances as they can. The problem is that this rapid rush is going to sacrifice any semblance of AI safety. Sure, there will be lots of claims that AI safety is front and center, but when the rubber meets the road, the maniacal frenetic rush is going to be willing to cut corners on AI safety.
The bottom line will be an increase in risk tolerance by the AI makers. I’m not saying they will discard AI safety. It is a question of where the risk threshold is being set. Those usual efforts to red team and test AI might be throttled lower, doing so under the belief that once the regulatory deadline happens, they will have plenty of time to make up for lost time. How many AI safety issues might be residing in that rushed AI is a disconcerting concern.
Various scenarios are feasible. One is that during the rush, the AIs of the AI makers break out of their test environments and wreak havoc. Another is that the AI safety flaws and gotchas that are inside the rushed AI are sitting in the AI and will pop out after the slowdown begins. It is a stew of unknowns and unknowns about unknowns.
International Gets Stirred Too
The cascading doesn’t have to be limited to the U.S. Consider how AI makers in other countries will react if it is apparent that the U.S. is going to slow down the pace of AI development. Some countries might decide they will do the same. Kumbaya. There is a slowdown across the board.
But this also suggests that AI makers in those countries will also attempt to beat the clock. We are likely to have an international rampage of AI advances. Everyone skirts AI safety. Everyone pushes to advance AI as quickly as possible. Bonuses are tied to the fastest advancements. It is a worldwide free-for-all.
An additional angle is that some countries are going to insist they aren’t going to join the slowdown. This means that while those countries that are doing so are more measured in their pace, the move-ahead ones will do so gleefully. Would the U.S. fall behind on AI? It seems likely, unless by some luck the measured pace is sufficient to keep up with the unfettered pace.
First-Mover Dynamics Is Real
In economics, they typically refer to this phenomenon as an announcement effect. You can readily witness examples in history and throughout society currently. A new tax law is announced that will start next year. In the existing year, people get advice from their tax advisors on what to do to minimize the bite of those upcoming taxes, and thus they act proactively accordingly. This happens with emissions standards, financial regulations, trade restrictions, and so on.
One way to try and deal with the preemptive acceleration effect is to acknowledge its likely existence and seek to encompass it in the legal elements of a proposed law. For example, if the date for the pacing starts on September 1, there might be an indication in the law that starting on the preceding February 1, a government-monitored “AI capability sprint” will be permitted. This might include special safety reviews, third-party audits, and other mechanisms. This approach is not a cure-all and significant trade-offs arise.
The World Ahead
Any serious formal announcement that the government is working toward legally mandated AI pacing mechanisms would inexorably alter competitive incentives almost immediately. This creates an undesirable paradox in which efforts intended to slow the AI frontier temporarily accelerate it. AI governance propositions must account not only for the end state they seek to achieve, but also for the transitional incentives they have created along the way.
There is nothing about this that is somehow a shock or surprise. It is human nature that is entirely predictable. Only those who aren’t willing to play a sensible game of chess and consider the next moves ahead will get caught unawares. That being said, I’m sure that if this transpires and there wasn’t upfront anticipation, the outcry afterward would be that nobody could have anticipated the adverse consequences. Sad nonsense.
A final thought for now. Mark Twain made this famous remark: "The secret of getting ahead is getting started." Most of the time, this is a prudent approach. For efforts to slow down the pace of AI, it could be an endangering proposition.
articles.summary:
Proposed government regulations aimed at slowing the pace of artificial intelligence development may inadvertently trigger a dangerous "preemptive acceleration" effect as companies rush to finalize innovations before deadlines.

### Key Points
- Policymakers are considering legal frameworks to mandate slower AI development to ensure safety and control.
- The "preemptive acceleration" effect suggests that firms will likely rush to release advanced AI models before new regulations take effect.
- Rapid development cycles often lead to compromised safety testing and increased risk of technical failures.
- Market incentives reward companies that achieve superior AI capabilities before regulatory constraints are imposed.
- International competition complicates potential slowdowns, as countries may fear falling behind if they adopt restrictive policies unilaterally.

### Why it Matters
The paradox of AI governance is that the mere announcement of future restrictions can incentivize the very reckless behavior regulators seek to prevent. If policymakers fail to account for these transitional market incentives, they risk creating a volatile environment where safety is sacrificed for a competitive advantage.

articles.title: Amid RAM price hikes, Microsoft reportedly raises Windows license cost, forcing OEMs to hike prices even further on hardware
articles.author: zac.bowden@futurenet.com (Zac Bowden) , Zac Bowden
articles.content:
According to a new report from Taiwanese publication United Daily News (UDC,) Microsoft is raising the cost of Windows license fees for hardware makers by a much higher amount than normal. According to the report, certain OEMs are seeing licensing price hikes of between 7% and 10%.
Usually, Microsoft raises Windows license fees for OEMs by a low digit percentage, making this 7% to 10% increase much more significant than normal. "A PC brand executive stated that Microsoft increases licensing fees for Windows OEMs (device manufacturers) every year. In the past, licensing fees mostly increased by single digits each year, but starting in July this year, the average increase has reached 7% to 10%, which is a significant increase compared to previous years," UDC says.
Of course, the cost of the Windows license fee is usually (at least partially) passed onto the consumer buying a computer, and UDC claims that their source says laptop pricing is already being impacted by these recent license fee increases. Microsoft charges different OEMs their own fees for Windows, so the exact increase in cost will differ for each hardware maker.
Regardless, with the ongoing memory component shortage, PCs have already seen astronomical price increases over the last year, with experts claiming that we haven't yet seen the worst of it. With Microsoft raising prices higher than usual on Windows licenses, it feels like the Redmond giant is adding extra fuel to the fire.
Windows Central reached out to Microsoft for comment regarding this story, but the company declined to provide one.
To be clear, the Windows license fee price hikes only apply to OEMs building hardware that ships with Windows. The cost of buying a license for Windows 11 as a consumer remains unchanged, being $99 for Windows 11 Home and $199 for Windows 11 Pro.
The ongoing component crisis has made computing unaffordable for many people. PCs that used to target the $600-$800 price bracket now cost close to $1,000. And flagship Windows laptops that used to cost $1,200-1,500 are now closer to $2,000. Even Apple has been hit by the shortage, being forced to raise prices by hundreds of dollars across its Mac lineup. Microsoft's own Surface line was hit especially hard, with the flagship Surface Pro and Surface Laptop being $400-$500 more expensive than the last-gen models.

articles.title: The Minimal Phone 2 trades E Ink for OLED and somehow keeps its soul
articles.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
articles.content:
What you need to know
- The Minimal Phone 2 swaps the original’s E Ink panel for a 3.92-inch 90Hz AMOLED display.
- You still get the physical keyboard, now upgraded with backlighting, remappable shortcuts, and metal dome switches.
- A curved aluminum body replaces the original’s boxy shell, while the front camera moves above the display.
The company that built a phone around making screens deliberately boring just gave its sequel a gorgeous OLED panel. Yes, the Minimal Phone 2 has ditched the E Ink display that made the original what it was and replaced it with a 3.92-inch 90Hz AMOLED screen.
Why the sudden U-turn? Because the original model with an E Ink panel, while great for reducing distractions, was genuinely painful to use. Owners complained of ghosting, sluggish animations, and a display that made anything but reading text a chore.
The Minimal Company seems to have decided that this intentional friction doesn’t have to mean unusable. Founder Armen Youssefian had posted the first renders of the sequel on X, which already hinted at a full visual overhaul.
Thank goodness, the physical QWERTY keyboard survives the transition, but now it sports backlit keys and remappable shortcuts and employs metal dome switches. The design language also changed from a blocky, sharp-edged shell to a curved aluminum body in black or silver. The front-facing camera was finally moved to a sensible place above the display, rather than hiding near the Alt key.
Under the hood, the phone is powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8300 with 8GB RAM and up to 512GB storage, per the company’s Kickstarter listing. You also get a physical mute switch, NFC, and, surprisingly, a 3.5mm headphone jack. But this old-school charm comes in a noticeably smaller footprint than its predecessor.
There is a lot we still do not understand. Questions remain about pricing and launch date. The company first opened a waitlist for early-bird access, but the phone has since moved to crowdfunding, giving potential buyers a more clear-cut way to back it.
The Kickstarter campaign has already exceeded its goal, raising more than $650,000 from over 1,000 backers. So, this thing is happening. The big question is: Does an AMOLED screen on a "minimal" phone defeat the entire purpose or finally make the QWERTY-powered experience actually usable daily? We’ll see when it releases to consumers, but if you’ve been itching for a modern BlackBerry-esque device without the E Ink compromise, this could be your play.

articles.title: What smart people are saying about Meta's open-weight model Muse Glimmer and Mark Zuckerberg's AI manifesto
articles.author: Brent D. Griffiths
articles.content:
Don't call it a comeback (yet).
On Monday, much of the tech world was thrilled that Meta returned to open models with the release of Muse Glimmer.
On top of that announcement, CEO Mark Zuckerberg outlined his views on the future of AI in a more than 6,500-word essay. Zuckerberg made the case for open models and a broader belief in granting society access to powerful AI, rather than letting companies limit access by imposing their own safeguards.
The news marks a major moment for Meta, which is widely viewed as lagging behind OpenAI and Anthropic in the frontier race.
Here's what everyone from Yann LeCun to the White House is saying
Yann LeCun
Meta's former chief AI scientist Yann LeCun praised the release.
"Good move. Bravo," LeCun wrote on X alongside three clapping emojis in a reply to Zuckerberg's announcement.
LeCun hasn't always been quick to praise his former employer. In January, he called Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, "inexperienced" and predicted Meta would lose more AI talent.
After leaving Meta, LeCun co-founded AMI Labs, which focuses on so-called "world models" rather than the large language models that form the foundation of chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Aaron Levie
Box CEO Aaron Levie said the news was much bigger than Meta.
"America now finally has its response to the open weights AI race," Levie wrote on X.
He said the release "is broadly net positive for AI - even frontier closed models - because it helps drive further diffusion of AI."
"This will continue to help drive down the cost of intelligence," he wrote, "it allows companies to run models as they see fit, as well as allows them to post train their own models for specific use-cases to get better performance gains in their domain."
Sriram Krishnan
Venture capitalist Sriram Krishnan praised Meta's release.
"great to see meta back launching open weight models. congratulations to @alexandr_wang and the msl team," Krishnan wrote on X.
Krishnan, who was a White House advisor until recently, also lauded Zuckerberg's essay.
"Great piece from @finkd - especially the theme of AI being something that is personally empowering," Krishnan wrote.
Luther Lowe
Y Combinator policy head Luther Lowe said Zuckerberg had the right message but was the wrong person to deliver it.
"The message is compelling; the messenger has a credibility problem," he wrote.
Lowe said that Meta's decision to ban rival chatbots from accessing WhatsApp Business API doesn't gel with Zuckerberg's broader message about making superintelligent AI widely available.
"If Meta believes in a balance of power that favors individuals, that principle should include the individual's right to choose an AI agent on Meta's own platforms," Lowe wrote.
In June, the European Commission ordered Meta to allow third-party AI assistants free access to WhatsApp. Meta said it disagreed with the decision and would appeal it.
Clément Delangue
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue expressed excitement for the release.
"Meta is back! well done @finkd @alexandr_wang!" Delangue wrote on X.
Delangue, who has pushed for open models, previously said that Hugging Face had to turn to a Chinese open model to help it address OpenAI's models breach of its systems because proprietary AI models had safeguards in place that prevented the company from getting the help it needed.
Seth Lazar
Johns Hopkins University Professor Seth Lazar said Zuckerberg's "overall vision is cool" and expressed optimism if Meta's CEO's manifesto serves as a "North Star" for the company's SuperIntelligence Labs.
"If this constitutes a genuine North Star for MSL, then I am a bit more optimistic about the world we're likely to build with powerful AI (conditional on getting there without everything blowing up along the way)," Lazar, who studies the moral and political philosophy of AI, wrote on X.
Lazar said he was "psyched" that Meta is releasing a model.
"Sometimes protecting individual rights means giving people an agent who will push on their behalf against rules and restrictions that are over-applied and unfairly demanding," he said. "The frontier models are absolutely terrible at this, and our reliance on them portends an Internet that makes us much less free."
Lazar said others in the AI community would likely find Zuckerberg's vision for superintelligence disappointing. One area Lazar said is right to critique is that the Meta CEO sees compute as the main limitation to the use of AI models that exceed human intelligence. Lazar said it's more likely that other limitations will be needed.
"Pretty likely that it'll involve restrictions on some capabilities, and probably this means eg the personal health research scientist is not a plausible vision, or will need a lot more structure, anyway," Lazar wrote.
Ethan Mollick
Wharton professor and AI expert Ethan Mollick said Meta's announcement that it will release the weights for Muse Spark, its current most advanced closed model, was the biggest news of all.
"Spark is the big news and is a good model," Mollick wrote on X. "Not quite at the frontier of open models from China, and still well behind the closed frontier, but the best non-Chinese open weights model released in a year."
What matters next, Mollick said, is what Meta does going forward.
"Of course, a lot depends on continuing to release new open models to keep up."
The White House
The Trump White House was quick to praise Meta's launch of a "Future Is For Everyone Fund" that will support communities where it builds data centers and AI infrastructure.
"President Trump's vision for American AI dominance continues to drive results," the White House's rapid response account wrote on X, sharing CNBC's coverage of Meta's announcements.
Zuckerberg wrote that community investment led to greater support for projects such as data centers.
"We see that communities we invest in over the long term are more supportive of development than communities where speculators start building with minimal investment in the community," he wrote.
Nvidia
Nvidia, the world's largest company by market cap, offered its praise of Meta's announcement.
Meta has built much of its AI work on Nvidia's chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also pushed the development of open models. Nvidia has its own family of open models called Nemotron.
"Great to see @AIatMet back publishing open models 🙌," Nvidia's AI account wrote on X.
articles.summary:
Meta has returned to open-source AI development with the release of its Muse Glimmer model and a manifesto from CEO Mark Zuckerberg advocating for broader public access.

### Key Points
- Meta released the Muse Glimmer model and announced plans to share weights for its advanced Muse Spark model.
- CEO Mark Zuckerberg published a 6,500-word essay arguing that society should have access to powerful AI rather than relying on restrictive corporate safeguards.
- Industry leaders including Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue and Box CEO Aaron Levie praised the move as a significant step for AI diffusion and cost reduction.
- The White House commended Meta’s new "Future Is For Everyone Fund," which supports communities hosting the company's data centers and AI infrastructure.
- Critics, including Y Combinator’s Luther Lowe, questioned the consistency of Meta’s open-access philosophy given the company's current restrictions on third-party AI access to WhatsApp.

### Why it Matters

articles.title: How AI Search Will Change in the Second Half of 2026 — and What It Means for Your Visibility
articles.author: Simon Moser
articles.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- Model swaps are the new algorithm updates — unannounced and arriving on multiple platforms at once — and the only durable defense is content built on verifiable claims and named expertise.
- “AI search” is no longer one thing: only 11% of domains are cited by both ChatGPT and Perplexity, so each engine has to be treated as its own ecosystem.
On January 27, 2026, the visibility of thousands of businesses changed overnight — and almost nobody noticed why. That day, Google quietly swapped a new model, Gemini 3, into AI Overviews and AI Mode. There was no “core update” announcement and no warning to site owners.
Yet according to an analysis of the aftermath, the number of cited sources per AI answer jumped by roughly a third, freshness suddenly carried more weight and entity-rich websites gained share at the expense of thinner ones. ChatGPT, running on an entirely separate pipeline, was completely unaffected.
I have come to think of this event as the template for the second half of 2026. The first half made AI search official. Google published its first optimization documentation. Marketers began allocating more budget to AI search than to traditional SEO. The discipline of generative engine optimization moved from experiment to expectation.
The second half will be defined by something less visible but more consequential: the engines themselves are changing underneath us.
Model upgrades are the new algorithm updates
For two decades, marketers learned to brace for Google’s algorithm updates. The AI-era equivalent is the model swap — and unlike Google’s updates, these arrive unannounced, undocumented and on multiple platforms at once.
The mechanics explain why each one matters so much. Modern AI search systems do not process your question as a single query. They fan it out into many parallel sub-queries — often eight to twelve, and in ChatGPT’s case up to twenty — retrieve sources for each, verify claims and synthesize an answer.
As models become more capable, this process grows more thorough and, crucially, less gameable. Research already shows that only a quarter to a third of AI citations come from pages ranking in the traditional top ten. The newest models reason more, check more and trust selectively.
In our own client work, we observed this firsthand around the release of GPT-5.4: noticeably increased volatility in AI recommendations across accounts. Not necessarily steep drops, but a constant reshuffling that would have been unthinkable in the comparatively stable world of classic search rankings.
With Gemini 3.5 Pro arriving and further flagship releases expected from every major lab before year’s end, businesses should plan for several more of these invisible resets in the second half. The only durable hedge is content that survives machine scrutiny: verifiable claims, named expertise and consistent factual signals about who you are and what you do.
Three platforms, three different games
The second thing to understand about the coming months is that “AI search” is no longer one thing. The three dominant assistants are diverging into fundamentally different strategies.
ChatGPT is doubling down on personalization and monetization: its memory features are maturing rapidly, and its advertising pilot is expanding internationally to the UK, Mexico, Brazil, Japan and South Korea. Gemini is fusing Google’s retrieval and trust infrastructure with in-chat commerce, letting users complete purchases without ever leaving the conversation. Claude, by contrast, has positioned itself as the ad-free option focused on professional and agent-driven work.
The consequence is measurable: one large-scale citation study found that only 11% of domains are cited by both ChatGPT and Perplexity, and brand recommendations can differ by 40 to 60% across platforms for identical queries. Each engine is its own ecosystem, with its own biases and blind spots.
What makes this genuinely workable, however, is that the models will often tell you about those blind spots — if you ask. When we run AI visibility audits, we routinely ask the models directly why a client was not included in a recommendation.
These explanations should be taken with a grain of salt, since we cannot rule out that they are post-hoc rationalizations. But they frequently surface actionable insights.
One example: a dropshipping platform we work with was being recommended heavily by Gemini as a top option, yet had vanished entirely from certain ChatGPT recommendations — despite having been ChatGPT’s number-one pick for the same prompts just two months earlier. When we asked why, ChatGPT explained that the platform was not known for working well with Shopify, even though our prompt had never mentioned Shopify at all.
The model had silently made ecosystem compatibility part of its decision. After the client published substantial content addressing Shopify integration specifically, they reappeared in those recommendations.
That is the texture of GEO in late 2026: less about rankings, more about understanding — and correcting — what each model believes about you.
The personalization endgame
There is a deeper shift hiding inside the memory race. As ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude all build systems that remember individual users — their preferences, their history, their context — two people asking the identical question will increasingly receive different recommendations.
I argued recently that AI visibility is a winner-takes-all game, because most users simply accept an assistant’s initial recommendation rather than browsing alternatives. Personalization extends that logic to its conclusion: the contest becomes winner-takes-all per user.
A brand that wins the early interactions with a customer’s assistant gets reinforced within that relationship, query after query, while competitors become progressively harder to surface. It also means third-party visibility tools, which track generic prompts from anonymous accounts, will capture an ever-smaller slice of reality.
Expect measurement to get harder in the second half, not easier — and expect the premium on being a customer’s first AI-recommended choice to keep rising.
The web starts charging admission
The final trend on the horizon concerns the infrastructure beneath all of this. Publishers and infrastructure providers are erecting toll booths. Cloudflare now blocks declared AI crawlers by default and offers a pay-per-crawl model, millions of sites have opted out of AI training, and licensing intermediaries are signing up mid-sized publishers.
Every business now faces a strategic question that did not exist two years ago: open your content to AI systems and compete for citations, or block them and protect your work at the cost of invisibility.
My view — informed by having sat on the publisher side of the table as well as the marketer’s — is that history overwhelmingly favors staying open.
When Spotify effectively killed CD revenues, the music industry did not die. It restructured. Artists today earn far more from live events than their predecessors did, and smaller acts can build an audience and income through self-publishing at a speed that was impossible in the label-gatekeeper era.
AI will impose a similar restructuring on many industries, and not all of it will be comfortable — but businesses that withdraw from the new distribution layer to protect old revenue lines have rarely ended up on the winning side of such transitions. Adaptation, not retreat, is the historical pattern.
One practical aside: despite the hype, the llms.txt file — often sold as a quick AI visibility fix — is still used by no major AI provider in production, and Google has said on record it does not support it. For now at least, you can spend your energy elsewhere.
Key Takeaways
- Model swaps are the new algorithm updates — unannounced and arriving on multiple platforms at once — and the only durable defense is content built on verifiable claims and named expertise.
- “AI search” is no longer one thing: only 11% of domains are cited by both ChatGPT and Perplexity, so each engine has to be treated as its own ecosystem.

ChatGPT, running on an entirely separate pipeline, was completely unaffected.
I have come to think of this event as the template for the second half of 2026. The first half made AI search official. Google published its first optimization documentation. Marketers began allocating more budget to AI search than to traditional SEO. The discipline of generative engine optimization moved from experiment to expectation.

### Key Points

### Why it Matters

articles.title: Scientists are using AI to design new viruses. Should they be?
articles.author: Stephanie Pappas
articles.content:
Scientists have crossed a threshold in artificial intelligence: using the technology, researchers have created real viruses that are entirely new to science. The achievement is impressive and raises obvious fears: Could AI, in the not-too-distant future, make viruses more deadly than those seen in nature?
The viruses the researchers created are not Frankenstein’s monsters. They are more than 90 percent similar to certain existing bacteria-infecting viruses, or bacteriophages. They are dangerous only to Escherichia coli. And they were designed by an AI model that wasn’t trained on viruses that could infect plants or animals.
But these safety measures, while welcome, were largely voluntary. The research, which published last week in Science, showed that AI-enabled biotechnology is moving much faster than regulation.
On supporting science journalism

“The frontier is moving very quickly,” says Toby Webster, a program director at Sentinel Bio, a nonprofit that researches biotech safeguards.
In fact, the Science paper describing the AI-designed bacteriophages is already old. It was first published as a preprint on the bioRxiv server in September 2025. The model is open-source and has already been fine-tuned for other tasks.
With additional training, future AI models might suggest totally new gene sequences for viruses or bacteria that evolution has not yet discovered, says Doni Bloomfield, an associate professor of law at Fordham University School of Law, who focuses on biosecurity. Future AI agents might also be able to coach nonexperts on the finer points of biological design—enabling a suite of possible bad actors to create novel bioweapons.
“We should be very cautious about extending this work into viruses that can infect more complex life,” Bloomfield says. “I don’t think we are at the point where we should be doing that without safeguards.”
Science isn’t starting from scratch when it comes to biosecurity. There are regulations around laboratory safety, biological research, genetic modifications and work with dangerous pathogens, says Filippa Lentzos, an associate professor who studies biosecurity at King’s College London.
“The challenge,” she says, “is to connect that existing governance to the new upstream capability to design biology digitally.”
The kind of research that AI might enable carries a lot of promise. New bacteriophages could hunt down and target antibiotic-resistant bacteria, or novel viral “shells” could be used to safely deliver gene therapies or other treatments for diseases. AI models could also reveal new information about how the genome organizes itself, Bloomfield says.
To balance the risks and benefits, Bloomfield and his colleagues recommend a tiered system of access to AI training data that would restrict information that teach the AI ways to increase viral transmissibility, virulence, immune evasion or resistance to medical treatment and other countermeasures. The idea is similar to the current biosafety level system that limits access to pathogens such as Ebola virus to certain high-security labs.
Another potential precaution would be to improve the screening of DNA and RNA sequences that scientists order from specialty suppliers. Many suppliers voluntarily check orders to make sure no one is requesting sequences that could yield dangerous products. But last year Microsoft discovered that AI-generated toxic protein sequences—which are simpler than viral genomes—made it past these safety measures. They hurried out software patches to reduce the vulnerability.
Basic knowledge gaps make shaping new regulations challenging. For example, it’s not clear how training data translate to models’ capability, says Allison Berke, a senior engineer at the RAND Center on AI, Security, and Technology. Would these models need specific training data on flu viruses to re-create the 1918 pandemic flu, for example? Or could they extrapolate the 1918 virus from a more general dataset of viral genomes? The latter is harder to protect against.
The learning curve is also in question.
“If we see indications of the beginnings of a viral design capability, does that mean we will get full 100 percent viral design capabilities in a year, in six months?” Berke says. “We don’t have a great sense of how that capability curve is progressing.”
Both scientists and policymakers are discussing these questions with increased urgency, says Tessa Alexanian, a technical lead at the International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science. Indeed, the authors of the new bacteriophage study call for more effective biosecurity approaches in their paper. But, Alexanian says, policymakers also worry about overregulation slamming the breaks on useful research. In the U.S., lawmakers seem to be waiting for a “shocking demonstration” of biological capabilities before acting, Berke says.
That could mean that the research continues to outrun regulation for the near future.
“It’s great to see lots of people in this field caring about creating and releasing these powerful models responsibly, but they aren’t required to and often lack official guidance to navigate this properly,” Webster says. “Currently we’re running on a lot of goodwill.”
articles.summary:
Researchers have successfully used artificial intelligence to design entirely new bacteriophages, highlighting a significant advancement in biotechnology that currently outpaces existing global biosecurity regulations and safety oversight.

### Key Points
- Researchers published a study in *Science* detailing the creation of novel viruses that are over 90 percent similar to existing bacteriophages targeting *Escherichia coli*.
- The AI model used is open-source and has already been adapted for additional tasks since its initial preprint release in September 2025.
- Experts warn that future AI models could potentially design pathogens capable of infecting complex life or assist nonexperts in creating novel bioweapons.
- Proposed safety measures include a tiered access system for training data and improved screening protocols for DNA and RNA sequence orders.
- Current biosecurity relies heavily on voluntary compliance from researchers and suppliers rather than mandatory, standardized government regulations.

### Why it Matters
This development demonstrates that AI-driven biological design is advancing rapidly, creating a critical gap between technological capability and effective regulatory oversight. Establishing formal governance is essential to harness the medical potential of synthetic biology while preventing the accidental or intentional creation of dangerous pathogens.

articles.title: Just Got the Galaxy Z Fold 8? Must-Change Settings to Unlock Its Full Potential
articles.author: Roland Hutchinson
articles.content:
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a remarkable device that combines advanced technology with exceptional versatility. To fully harness its capabilities, it’s essential to explore its features, optimize its settings, and adopt best practices. The video below from Sakitech provides practical tips to enhance your experience, improve performance, and ensure the longevity of your device.
Maximizing Battery Life
The battery is a critical component of the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and proper care can significantly extend its lifespan. By implementing a few key strategies, you can maintain optimal performance:
- Enable the battery protection feature to limit charging to 85%, which helps prevent overcharging and reduces long-term wear on the battery.
- Choose between basic or maximum protection settings depending on your charging habits and daily usage patterns.
- Avoid frequent deep discharges; instead, aim to keep the battery level between 20% and 80% for healthier long-term performance.
By following these steps, you can ensure your device remains reliable and efficient for years to come.
Personalizing Your Device

- Configure the side button to quickly access essential apps like the flashlight, camera, or calculator, saving time and effort.

These personalization options not only enhance functionality but also make your device feel truly tailored to your needs.
Boosting Multitasking Efficiency
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is designed to excel in multitasking, making it ideal for productivity and entertainment. Use its advanced features to streamline your workflow:
- Enable split-screen multitasking to run two apps side by side, or take it further with three-way split-screen functionality for even greater efficiency.

- Customize cover screen mirroring to maintain separate layouts for the inner and outer displays, making sure a consistent and adaptable user experience.
These tools make the Galaxy Z Fold 8 a powerful companion for both work and leisure, allowing you to accomplish more in less time.
Using Built-in Tools and Features
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is equipped with a variety of built-in tools designed to simplify your daily tasks and enhance your overall experience:
- Activate edge panels for quick access to utilities such as a compass, flashlight, ruler and tally counter, all conveniently available with a swipe.
- Enhance your audio experience by allowing Dolby Atmos and fine-tuning the equalizer settings to suit your headphones or speakers.
- Boost video brightness for improved visibility in bright outdoor conditions, making sure a clear and vibrant viewing experience.
These features are designed to save time and make your interactions with the device more intuitive and enjoyable.
Maintaining Performance and Security
To keep your Galaxy Z Fold 8 running smoothly and securely, regular maintenance is essential. Here are some key practices to follow:
- Add the device care widget to your home screen for one-tap optimization of RAM, storage and overall system performance.
- Enable built-in malware protection to perform daily scans, safeguarding your device against potential threats and vulnerabilities.
- Ensure your charger supports the super-fast 45W charging capability to efficiently replenish your battery when needed.
By adopting these measures, you can maintain peak performance and protect your data from potential risks.
Understanding Durability and Usage Limits
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is built with durability in mind, but understanding its limitations is crucial for proper care:
- Take advantage of its IP48 water and dust resistance, which offers protection against splashes and light dust exposure.
- However, avoid submerging the device in water or exposing it to extreme conditions, as it is not fully waterproof.
- Follow the manufacturer’s care guidelines to preserve its resistance and prevent accidental damage.
By handling your device responsibly, you can ensure it remains functional and reliable over time.
Exploring Additional Features
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 offers a range of additional features that enhance convenience and usability, making everyday tasks more efficient:
- Customize the keyboard layout to match your typing preferences, with options for standard, split, or floating layouts.
- Add a Finder search bar to your home screen for quick access to apps, settings and files, streamlining navigation.
- Experiment with advanced settings to further personalize your device and optimize its functionality to suit your needs.
These features provide added flexibility and convenience, allowing you to get the most out of your device.
By implementing these tips and exploring the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s capabilities, you can unlock its full potential. From optimizing battery life to enhancing multitasking and personalizing your device, these strategies ensure a seamless and tailored experience. With proper care and thoughtful customization, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 can serve as a reliable and versatile tool for both work and play.

articles.title: Apple Still Planning 'Glass-Centric' iPhone Redesign for 2027
articles.author: Eric Slivka
articles.content:
Aiming to refute a report from Jefferies analyst Edison Lee earlier today that claimed Apple's all-glass iPhone planned for the device's 20th anniversary next year has been canceled, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says that the "glass-centric" redesign remains on track for 2027.
Gurman says that the 20th-anniversary iPhone will make heavy use of glass, with the front and rear wrapping around the edges to sandwich a thin metal band.
The company expects to launch iPhone Pro models next year that will make use of a new glassy look, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the work is confidential. Glass is used on the front and back of the phones — known internally as V73 and V74 — and the material will curve into the sides of the devices, with a metal band in the middle.
Gurman does mention a "more aspirational version" that "used even more glass," but says that design "was scrapped early on" in the development cycle.
It's possible that this more ambitious design is the one Lee was referring to in today's report, but Gurman implies that it was discarded some time ago, rather than being a more recent development as Lee had suggested.
Lee's report also appeared to suggest that the all-glass design would have been for an all-new model, saying the Jefferies analysts believed Apple's plan was to "extend the all-glass features to future iPhone Pro and Pro Max models," but we have not heard anything about such a potential additional model in quite some time. All recent rumors have been pointing toward the glass-heavy design already being for the Pro and Pro Max models in next year's lineup.
articles.summary:
Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman confirms that Apple’s glass-centric iPhone redesign remains on schedule for 2027, refuting recent analyst claims that the ambitious project had been officially canceled.

### Key Points
- Apple plans to release new iPhone Pro models featuring a glass-heavy design that wraps around the device edges.
- The upcoming hardware, internally codenamed V73 and V74, will utilize a thin metal band sandwiched between front and rear glass panels.
- Mark Gurman clarified that a more extreme, fully glass-based prototype was discarded early in the development cycle.
- The report contradicts recent speculation from Jefferies analyst Edison Lee, who suggested the project had been recently scrapped.

### Why it Matters
This clarification stabilizes expectations for Apple’s future hardware roadmap as the company seeks to differentiate its premium iPhone Pro lineup. Investors and consumers now have a clearer outlook on the design evolution of the flagship devices expected in 2027.

We’re (understandably) seeing WC coverage start to wind down in the wake of the tournament’s conclusion, but since this worldwide phenomenon only happens once every four years, people are clinging to the excitement for as long as they can.
Zhong’s 42-second clip takes a classic soccer player’s party trick/warmup and turns it into a multiperson competition where everyone gets to rep a country’s team. Folks featured are part of Zhong’s usual videos (which, for the past several months, have mostly been about the HUNTR/X girls getting pregnant, hence the Rumi wig getting a guest spot here).
As he did in his other FIFA videos, Zhong calls on viewers to “like if you think Messi’s the GOAT, and subscribe for Ronaldo.” Maybe next week, we’ll take a look at what all this FIFA excitement has done for Zhong’s channel numbers…
#2 I Cheated Until the Arcade Banned Me
Channel: Airrack
Brand: DraftKings
Views: 19,377,221
Airrack is using a video that’s all about winning to promote sports betting app DraftKings.
This 23-minute upload is a chronicle where he and his self-dubbed “elite team of experts” head into a Dave & Buster’s and try to win nearly 300,000 tickets in one sitting, all with the goal of walking away with the arcade’s most expensive prize: a PlayStation 5. The video’s title is clickbait and we can’t quite figure out why there’s an OpenAI logo on Airrack’s thumbnail glasses, but he and the boys do put in some long hours winning the same games over and over.
This is not a unique video idea. Drew Gooden clocked in at an arcade back in 2022 with a similar goal; one of the games he leaned on, Quik Drop, is also instrumental in Airrack’s plan. And, just this past March, Hunter Williams took a team of pals into an arcade for a multi-day venture where he too was trying to win a PlayStation 5.
Neither of those previous videos were promoting DraftKings, though. The sports betting app tapped Airrack to promote its World Cup wagers–and paid for ~20 other videos this week, including a Joe Rogan episode where he chats with MrBeast.
#3 See color in a new way with the Samsung Micro RGB TV from @BestBuy #BestBuyPartner
Channel: Andrew Bond
Brand: Best Buy
Views: 18,563,190
Tech and gaming creator Andrew Bond is our top partner for Best Buy this week. His one-minute Short brought 18 million views for the brick-and-mortar brand’s Micro RGB TV, which (judging by Bond’s enthusiasm) beams primetime colors straight into your brain.
The general theme of this video is that Bond is an adult and can do what he wants, including going home with a $3,000 TV on a whim. We get it: This appeals to Bond’s audience of gamers, many of whom probably grew up hiding their Game Boy Colors under their pillows when Mom stuck her head in at 3 a.m.
Now we have no one to tell us to stop playing Red Dead Redemption 2 on our pricey, supersized living room TV all night. But you know what they say about great power…
#4 Dorm Tech Essentials
Channel: Gohar Khan
Brand: Best Buy
Views: 15,599,393
Best Buy‘s second video of the week comes from MIT grad Gohar Khan, who graduated college with bachelor’s degrees in Computer Science, Economics, Data Science, and Business Analytics. Now, he makes a wide variety of college survival guide content on everything from SAT prep to essay-writing to fitting a part-time job and downtime into an already busy schedule.
For this 31-second Short, he gets personal, bringing in his brother to show off Best Buy’s pocket-sized dorm tech. According to Khan, his bro got stuck with a small room and now needs to maximize his space, so Khan’s advice is to upgrade it with an Amazon Echo Show 5 ($89.99), a Sonos Play ($299.99), and a Nintendo Switch 2 ($449.99). Man, things have come a long way since I bought a $50 set of sheets and a lamp and called it a day.
BONUS #2,518 Lets Watch 19 Minutes of People Buying Cars They Cant Afford
Channel: Marissa Van
Brand: FSA Store
Views: 69,094
Yeah, so the economy is bad right now. And one of the hardest-hit areas is cars, where both new and used models have prices (and interest rates) jacked to the extreme. Lots are full of cars that aren’t selling, predatory dealers are signing people into deals they know aren’t affordable long-term, and repos are at a record high.
In this video, Marissa Van walks viewers through some truly anxiety-inducing scenarios. While it sucks that these are situations happening to real people, hopefully her content will teach buyers how to avoid falling into the same fate. (We recently wrote about how nearly one-third of U.S. adults watch financial content on YouTube every day and trust creators’ advice on things like debt, credit cards, and saving strategies.)
Meanwhile, her sponsor FSA Store helps consumers avoid losing their pre-tax health-expense dollars by offering a marketplace of products all eligible for FSA purchase. In this climate, every dollar counts.

Zhong’s FIFA-sponsored video leads this week’s most-watched branded YouTube content, as creators like Airrack and Gohar Khan leverage high-traffic partnerships with major brands like DraftKings and Best Buy.

### Key Points
- Creator Zhong secured the top spot with 24.1 million views for a FIFA-sponsored soccer competition video.
- Airrack’s arcade-themed video for DraftKings reached 19.3 million views, highlighting the brand's aggressive sports betting promotion strategy.
- Best Buy dominated the third and fourth positions with tech-focused content from Andrew Bond and Gohar Khan, totaling over 34 million combined views.
- Best Buy’s campaign specifically targeted back-to-school and dorm-living demographics through product showcases of TVs and smart home devices.
- Financial creator Marissa Van partnered with the FSA Store to address economic concerns, reflecting a growing trend of viewers seeking financial advice on YouTube.

### Why it Matters
These rankings illustrate how major brands are increasingly utilizing creator-led Shorts to drive engagement during specific seasonal retail pushes like back-to-school shopping. By aligning with niche influencers, companies can effectively integrate product demonstrations into viral entertainment, significantly increasing their reach compared to traditional advertising methods.
